newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Menem vows Argentine health-plan reform by decree.
newsitem.headline: Menem vows Argentine health-plan reform by decree.

text.p: Argentine President Carlos Menem vowed Tuesday to use his power of decree to deregulate the country's union-controlled health-care system to allow Argentines to choose their own medical plans.

"In the course of this week we will have news about the deregulation of social health care. This can be done by decree, not a decree of 'urgent necessity' but a simple decree. That's what we are working on," the Peronist leader said during a local radio broadcast.
Argentina currently has more than 300 union-controlled health plans financed by mandatory contributions, which bring in about $2.5 billion a year to the unions.

In the face of fierce union opposition, the government has been trying to eliminate compulsory affiliation with the union "obras sociales" since 1993. Many of the health plans are deep in debt, and members have had to seek duplicate coverage in private schemes.
"From next year we will be able to choose freely the most efficient and low-cost option for our healthcare," Menem said.
The subsidies currently cost the government about $200 million a year and go to 80 percent of the health plans, he said.

Health care is a major point of contention between Menem's government and trade unions. Though the Peronists and unions are traditional allies, they are already fighting over a bill sent to Congress late Monday to make labor legislation more flexible -- one of the issues behind a 36-hour general strike last week.
Santander said unions should listen to the opinion of their health-care members before opposing deregulation.

"There are polls that show that 80 percent of beneficiaries want free choice and not just those on high salaries, but more than 70 percent of a lower income bracket," he said. "They want free choice because service is poor."

The official said health-care programs were being offered cheap government loans at 3.0 percent a year over 12 years "to reorganize and streamline, and get their finances in shape." So far, they have failed to take advantage of the credit line, he said
